metadata.title: Unbearable Heat Suspected in 19 New Jersey Deaths as High Temperatures Give Way to Thunderstorms

sources.news_title: Unbearable heat suspected in 19 New Jersey deaths as high temperatures give way to thunderstorms
sources.text:
Several days of scorching temperatures are suspected to have caused at least 19 deaths in New Jersey as a heat dome that had settled above parts of the central and eastern United States gives way to severe storms that have knocked out power to close to 1 million homes and businesses.
New Jersey officials said Saturday that they began seeing what they believe are heat-related deaths as early as Thursday with most occurring in the central and northern parts of the state.
“Unfortunately, many of these individuals were found in homes without air conditioning,” state Health Commissioner Dr. Raynard Washington told reporters Saturday. “A few were outside their residences, some on the street and some even in parked cars.”
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill called the current weather “the hottest stretch we’ve seen in over 14 years.”
“The heat’s hitting all of us, not just seniors, not just with underlying health conditions, people of all ages,” Sherrill said.
On Thursday, LaGuardia Airport in New York set a new record high of 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius), topping the previous record of 101 F (38.3 C) set in 1966, according to Bryan Jackson, a meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Weather Prediction Center.
Trenton, New Jersey, reached 101 F, which broke the record of 100 F (37.7 C) set in 1901. Newark’s high Thursday was 105 F (40.5 C).
Atlantic City, New Jersey, hit 103 F (39.4 C) on Thursday, breaking the city’s record of 100 F set in 1966, Jackson said. Atlantic City reached 105 F on Friday and 106 F (41.1 C) on Saturday.
Heat domes can be dangerous and combine very high temperatures with high moisture, Jackson said.
“In a lot of cases they also had direct sunshine,” he said. “It was relentless. It was multiple days. It was not as cool overnight, as well. The low Friday morning in Atlantic City was 80. The body can’t recover as well. You just have that multiple day buildup and too much added stress on the body.”
But even as the heat moved to the east, lowering temperatures a bit, severe storms blew in with heavy winds that toppled utility poles and split trees, causing their boles and branches to fall onto power lines.
About 900,000 utility customers in parts of the central, eastern and southern United States were without electricity early Sunday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.com.
More than 223,000 customers in Michigan and close to 170,000 in Pennsylvania had lost power.
PPL Electric reported 121,417 without power Sunday morning, including about 47,000 in the Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, area.
Central Hudson in New York State reported that it had more than 430 reported downed wires on Sunday. The utility said about 50,000 customers were affected by the storm and that about 650 still were without power Sunday.
Amanda Vesper was putting her children to bed Friday evening when the first storm rolled through the Detroit area, knocking out her power.
“It didn’t seem that awful. It got quite windy,” said Vesper, 40, of Commerce Township.
As of late Sunday morning, the electricity still was out.
“We’ve been going back and forth between a hotel and our home because we have dogs there,” she said. “We really can’t stay there. I have a small child with autism. Our well runs on an electric pump.”
The outage also ruined the family’s July 4 celebration.
“We had planned on having company over at the house, but had to cancel,” Vesper said. “I went grocery shopping. I’m hoping my freezer holds.”
Jackson, with the Weather Prediction Center, said Sunday will see heavy thunderstorms in and around the Cleveland area. Those storms then will shift eastward and move into Pennsylvania, New Jersey and New York — where chances exist for flash flooding, he added.

sources.news_title: At least 19 suspected heat-related deaths in New Jersey as temps soar over the July 4th holiday
sources.text:
At least 22 suspected heat-related deaths in New Jersey as temps soar over the July 4th holiday
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on GoogleThere have been at least 22 suspected heat-related deaths across New Jersey as temperatures soared over the July 4 holiday, officials said.
“We started to see what we believed to be heat-related deaths as early as Thursday of this week… many of these individuals were found in homes without air conditioning,” New Jersey Department of Health Commissioner Dr. Raynard Washington said in a press briefing Saturday.
The metropolitan area experienced a historic heat wave heading into the July 4 holiday, with temperatures in New York City and the Garden State hitting record highs.
Central Park reached 100 degrees Thursday, tying it for the hottest day in the city since 1966. It was the first time the park hit triple digits since 2012. The Manhattan park reached 99 degrees the same time last year.
Brutal humidity and sweltering conditions left New Yorkers scrambling for shade as real-feel temperatures surged to as much as 110 degrees.
Big Apple subways have felt like an inferno with temperatures hitting the mid-to-high 90s in multiple subway lines, with real feels breaking 100 degrees and climbing.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged New Yorkers to keep their thermostats cranked up to a blistering 78 degrees amid the heatwave.
“New York: it’s hot out there, and the power grid is working overtime to keep us cool, set your AC to 78 degrees, turn off lights/electronics you’re not using, and unplug what you can,” Hizzoner wrote in a post on X.
New York City health officials said there were no confirmed heat-related deaths so far during the current heat wave.
“Tragically, we lose about 500 New Yorkers due to heat-related illness annually. That is why the Mamdani Administration is taking a whole-of-government response to extreme heat,” a city hall spokesperson said in a statement.
New Jersey wasn’t so lucky in terms of heat-wave fatalities, with at least 22 dead, NBC reported.
Even flash thunderstorms weren’t able to break the heat’s grip on the city.
Heat-fueled thunderstorms with winds of 60 mph punished the metro area and left thousands without power Friday.
Trees were downed onto cars in powerlines in Morris and Monmouth Counties in New Jersey, leaving some beleaguered residents trapped.
Over 10,000 New Yorkers lost power in Queens as a result of the storms.
But despite the cool air brought in from the tempests, the city still neared 100 degrees Saturday ahead of the big fireworks display.

sources.news_title: New Jersey suffers 19 suspected heat-related deaths since Thursday
sources.text:
New Jersey suffers 19 suspected heat-related deaths since Thursday
- Daytime temperatures are soaring between 95°F and 102°F across most local areas, with peak heat index values — how hot it actually feels outside — expected to hit between 105 and 110 degrees
- Service on the Morris and Essex, Gladstone Branch, Montclair-Boonton, and North Jersey Coast Lines are suspended due to ongoing repairs to infrastructure damage following last night’s severe storms
The brutal heave wave that has gripped the state and the Jersey Shore has caused 19 heat-related deaths, according to state officials.
At a news conference with Gov. Mikie Sherrill in Woodbridge on Saturday, Dr. Raynard E. Washington, commissioner for the state Department of Health, said there had been 19 suspected heat-related deaths in New Jersey since Thursday.
“With most of those being in the central to northern part of the state,” Washington said, but not elaborating more specifically.
Many of the victims were found in homes without air conditioning, a few were outside of their residence, some were in streets and some were in parked cars. He compared this death toll to last year's figure of six heat-related deaths.
Forecasters are warning of more record-shattering triple-digit heat, an official “Code Orange” air quality alert, and an increased threat of severe, flash-flood-producing thunderstorms just as Saturdday evening fireworks displays are scheduled to begin.
The National Weather Service in Mount Holly has maintained an extreme heat warning until 8 p.m. for Ocean, Monmouth, Middlesex, Somerset, and southeastern Burlington counties.
True to the forecast, daytime temperatures are soaring between 95°F and 102°F across most local areas, with peak heat index values — how hot it actually feels outside — expected to hit between 105 and 110 degrees through early this evening.
New Jersey Transit problems
NJ Transit said train service may need to operate at reduced speeds which could result in delays due to the heat. Additionally, service on the Morris and Essex, Gladstone Branch, Montclair-Boonton, and North Jersey Coast Lines are suspended due to ongoing repairs to infrastructure damage following last night’s severe storms, according to the state agency. Eight other lines are operating normally, state officials said
Meteorologists emphasize that this is a prolonged, cumulative heat event. Because overnight temperatures have only dropped into the mid-70s to low-80s, with the nighttime hours virtually offering little relief from the stifling humidity. The weather service explicitly noted that under these conditions, fans and open windows at night will be insufficient. Air conditioning will be a necessity to prevent heat-related illness.
Strong sunshine and extreme ground temperatures have driven pollution and ground-level ozone to levels that are unhealthy for sensitive groups, including children, the elderly, and anyone suffering from asthma or heart and lung diseases.
Possible local event disruptions
The severe weather setup has local officials on high alert. Many communities are warning that typical Fourth of July parades, outdoor concerts, and fireworks displays may be subject to last-minute weather postponements or cancellations. Residents are strongly urged to check with their local municipal websites or police department social media pages before heading out.
For those lacking air conditioning or trapped in areas still dealing with the lingering power outages from Friday night’s storms, local municipalities are stepping up.
In Ocean County, for example, the Point Pleasant Borough Hall at 2233 Bridge Avenue has been opened to the public as an active cooling center and will remain open until 5:00 PM today.
For a list of cooling centers in New Jersey that are near you, visit this site.
While the beach crowd may be praying for a cooling breeze, any relief arriving later today could come at a steep price. The weather service has increased its threat assessment for severe weather late this afternoon through tonight.
A 30% chance of isolated, fast-moving thunderstorms kicks in after 5 p.m., with storm chances jumping to a significant 70% tonight. Because the atmosphere is heavily charged with extreme heat and moisture, any storm that develops has the potential to produce damaging winds, frequent cloud-to-ground lightning, and torrential downpours.
Worse, confidence is increasing regarding the potential for widespread flash flooding. While tonight’s storms could drop up to half an inch of rain locally, forecasters are warning that Sunday afternoon and Sunday night bear an even higher risk for dangerous, localized inundations as a broader front moves over the saturated ground.
According to an analysis by USA TODAY, excessive temperatures over the Fourth of July holiday may not be common but they are also not unheard of:
Freehold: 100 in 1949, 1966
In both 1949 and 1966, Freehold experienced highs of 100 on Independence Day, according to the NWS. Within the years of recorded climate data, temperatures in the town haven't exceeded 100 on July 4. This year, the NWS expects temperatures to narrowly avoid beating that record, with a forecasted high of 99. Nighttime temperatures are expected to drop to 75, with a 40% chance of showers and storms.
Long Branch: 100 in 1949
Long Branch also experienced a July 4 high of 100 in 1949. This year, the NWS predicts daytime temperatures will soar up to 95 on the holiday. At night, temperatures are predicted to drop to a low of 76 with a 40% chance of precipitation.
Lakewood: 101 in 1949
In the same year, temperatures in Lakewood on the holiday rose to 101 degrees, the highest for the 4th in the NWS' recorded history of the town. This year, temperatures may soar to a nearly-triple-digit high of 99, dropping to 76 at night with a 50% chance of storms and rain.
Toms River: 103 in 1966
The highest recorded temperature on the list, Toms River experienced a record July 4th high of 103 in 1966. On Saturday, the town is expected to experience 99-degree heat during the day, with a nighttime low of 75 and a 50% chance of storms and rain.
Tuckerton: 102 in 1966
Similarly struck by the 1966 heatwave, Tuckerton hit a sizzling 102 on that year's Independence Day. Only slightly cooler, this year's high is expected to climb to 97, dropping to 75 at night with a 50% chance of precipitation.
With the entire population currently facing an “extreme risk” for heat exhaustion and heat stroke, emergency service officials and weather exerts recommend taking immediate, proactive measures:
- Hydrate constantly: Drink plenty of water and fluids; do not wait until you feel thirsty. Avoid alcohol and caffeine, which accelerate dehydration;
- Dress appropriately: Wear lightweight, loose-fitting, and light-colored clothing;
- Limit exposure: Cancel or significantly curtail outdoor activities during the peak afternoon heat. Strenuous work should be strictly restricted to the early morning or late evening hours;
- Never leave pets or children in motor vehicles: Vehicle interiors can reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes;
- Check on neighbors: Take a moment to check up on elderly neighbors, relatives, and those who live alone without reliable air conditioning.
If you or someone near you exhibits signs of heat stroke — such as confusion, a lack of sweating despite the heat, or loss of consciousness — call 911 immediately.
Contact Asbury Park Press reporter Erik Larsen at elarsen@gannettnj.com.

sources.news_title: 19 deaths in New Jersey likely connected to heat wave, officials say
sources.text:
The current heat wave gripping the tri-state has had deadly consequences in New Jersey.
Nineteen people across New Jersey have died in the first week of July, the state's health commissioner said Saturday.
"We started to see what we believe to be heat-related deaths as early as Thursday of this week," Dr. Raynard Washington said. "We are now up to 19 suspected heat-related deaths across the state, with most of those being in the central to northern part of the state."
Watch NBC 4 free wherever you are
Washington and Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who also attended the press conference, did not give any further information on the ages of those who had died. The health commissioner did stress the circumstances of those dead varied significantly.
"Unfortunately, many of these individuals were found in homes without air conditioning; few were outside of their residence, some on the street, and some even in parked cars," according to Washington.
Last year's heat wave resulted in six heat-related deaths, the health commissioner said.
The heat has not been the only weather factor in the region. The arrival of vicious storms late Friday knocked out power to thousands of utility customers, wrecked havoc on NJ Transit operations, and downs countless trees.
New Jersey news
From Newark to Trenton to Hoboken to Jersey City and all points between, NBC New York covers New Jersey news, weather, traffic and more.
By noon on July Fourth, temperatures across parts of the Northeast were already soaring back toward triple digits, resuming conditions likely to be relieved by the storms predicted to follow, leaving temperatures much lower for the start of a new week.

sources.news_title: 25 Dead as Extreme Heat Sweeps US
sources.text:
At least 25 people have died across the US amid an intense heat wave, including 22 fatalities in New Jersey, according to local health authorities.
Temperatures in Washington reached 38.8°C during Independence Day celebrations, breaking a record that had stood for more than a century. New York also recorded temperatures near 38°C, causing asphalt to soften in parts of the city.
Heat-related deaths were also reported in Illinois and Mississippi as extreme temperatures and severe weather strained power grids across several states.
More than 840,000 households were left without electricity on Saturday as the combination of scorching heat and storms disrupted energy supplies.
Several cities along the East Coast cancelled or postponed Fourth of July events because of the extreme weather, underscoring the growing impact of heat waves on public safety and infrastructure in the US.
